prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow. Physical infra- structure, e.g., traffic lights and raised medians (traffic islands) reduce vehicle–pedestrian collision frequency and severity (King, Carnegie, & Ewing, 2003; Stipancic, Miranda-Moreno, Strauss, & Labbe, 2020). But although physical crossing infrastructure that increases pedestrian safety can be implemented relatively cost-efficiently during the initial building of roads, the associated costs for the retroactive installation of physical road crossing infrastructure often leads to a preference for painted crosswalk markings (Stoker et al., 2015). In comparison to physical infrastructure, traditional, painted crosswalks can be installed with little resources. However, studies show that traditional marked crosswalks have little positive impact on pedestrian safety (Retting, Ferguson, & McCartt, 2003), and even increase pedestrian crash rates for some road environments (Zegeer, Stewart, Huang, & Lagerwey, 2001). In contrast to tradi- tional crosswalks, innovative crosswalk designs have more positive effects on pedestrian crash risk. High-visibility crosswalks, which use larger painted areas significantly increase pedestrian safety (Feldman, Manzi, & Mitman, 2010; Fitzpatrick, Chrysler, Iragavarapu, & Park, 2011; Guo, & Boyle, 2022; Pulugurtha, Vasudevan, Nambisan, & Dangeti, 2012; Sarwar et al., 2017). 1.1. 3D crosswalks The “3D zebra crossing” / “3D crosswalk” is a relatively new category of crosswalks which has not been investigated in depth for its effect on safety perceptions by road users. This type of crosswalk uses optical illusions to provoke the perception of a three-dimensional crosswalk from a vehicle driver’s perspective, even though the crosswalk markings are painted flat on the road. I.e., there is a dif- ference between the visual percept of road users (what they perceive) and the visual stimuli (reality). 3D crosswalks have been painted in several pilot projects around the world (e.g., in Aarhus, Denmark (Eurocities, 2021); Chiang Mai, Thailand (Pichayapan, Kaew- moracharoen, Peansara, & Nanthavisit, 2020); ´ Isafjo¨rður, Iceland (Iceland Magazine, 2017); or Montr´eal, Canada (Woods, 2018)). As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

The cycle lane is most positively rated on Physical Comfort and Ease of Use. Compared to the adjacent cycle path, the cycle lane has stronger lane markings which increases the Ease of Use for cyclists. Additionally, it runs on the road level next to the motor traffic and is usually better asphalted than cycle paths. This allows a more fluent cycling and increases the Physical Comfort. Interestingly, the cycle lane is rated slightly more negatively on Mental Comfort than on Interaction. A well marked cycle lane is often considered as a proper cycling facility that draws drivers’ attention to possible cyclists. However, although it separates from the motor traffic and, therefore, leads to less possible interactions, cyclists might perceive it as mentally uncomfortable because of a small width and a lack of feeling safe. Generally spoken, the less the cycling facility is separated the worse it is rated on the clusters. Surprisingly, the bicycle boulevard is evaluated similar to the least separated advisory lane, but with a much better rating in Mental Comfort. This indicates that a too weak separation can no longer induce a feeling of safety or Mental Comfort, and below this threshold of separation, cyclists might prefer bicycle boulevards which draw attention to cyclists as road users, but in principle have no separation at all. More concrete, cyclists may prefer no separation over a too weak one. Bicycle boulevards are also evaluated more positively than residential roads, although in Germany, bicycle boulevards are usually open for motorized traffic and the traffic regulations are, hence, the same as for residential roads. The only difference are traffic signs that highlight cyclists as road users who must not be endangered by motor vehicles, and that cyclists are allowed to cycle side by side (Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection, 2020). On the one hand, this may lead to a stronger self-confidence of the cyclists towards other road users. On the other hand, cyclists may associate a bicycle boulevard with even lower traffic volume, lower traffic speed, and more cooperative and careful interactions with other road users which increases their perception of Interaction, Environment, and Mental Comfort compared to the residential road. The shared footpath is evaluated neither good nor bad on all the clusters. The Mental and Physical Comfort are even lower than at bicycle boulevards and shared spaces. Cyclists may feel uncomfortable here as they cycle on a way which is mainly for walking, and cycling is only tolerated. Cyclists are, thus, in the position of the stronger road user that must be considerate towards the weaker and slower pedestrians. Also, cyclists need to watch out for people leaving buildings or properties and suddenly stepping onto the footpath. All this might be perceived as stressful and as hindering the cycling flow. Demographic information The survey collected age, gender, self-reported Geller typology, bicycling confidence and bike riding frequency (i.e., frequency per year/month/week) information. The Geller typology is a measure of comfort and willingness to ride in different infrastructure environments (Pearson et al., 2022). A single-item version was used in the present study (“In terms of your level of comfort while bike riding, how would you categorise yourself?”) (Hosford et al., 2020). Possible responses, in descending order of comfort and motivation, included: (a) ‘Strong and fearless’ (Comfortable cycling with traffic), (b) ‘Enthused and confident’ (Comfortable in traffic but prefer bike lanes and like using segregated facilities), (c) ‘Interested but concerned’ (Interested in cycling more but concerned about traffic and safety. Physical infra- structure, e.g., traffic lights and raised medians (traffic islands) reduce vehicle–pedestrian collision frequency and severity (King, Carnegie, & Ewing, 2003; Stipancic, Miranda-Moreno, Strauss, & Labbe, 2020). But although physical crossing infrastructure that increases pedestrian safety can be implemented relatively cost-efficiently during the initial building of roads, the associated costs for the retroactive installation of physical road crossing infrastructure often leads to a preference for painted crosswalk markings (Stoker et al., 2015). In comparison to physical infrastructure, traditional, painted crosswalks can be installed with little resources. However, studies show that traditional marked crosswalks have little positive impact on pedestrian safety (Retting, Ferguson, & McCartt, 2003), and even increase pedestrian crash rates for some road environments (Zegeer, Stewart, Huang, & Lagerwey, 2001). In contrast to tradi- tional crosswalks, innovative crosswalk designs have more positive effects on pedestrian crash risk. High-visibility crosswalks, which use larger painted areas significantly increase pedestrian safety (Feldman, Manzi, & Mitman, 2010; Fitzpatrick, Chrysler, Iragavarapu, & Park, 2011; Guo, & Boyle, 2022; Pulugurtha, Vasudevan, Nambisan, & Dangeti, 2012; Sarwar et al., 2017). 1.1. 3D crosswalks The “3D zebra crossing” / “3D crosswalk” is a relatively new category of crosswalks which has not been investigated in depth for its effect on safety perceptions by road users. This type of crosswalk uses optical illusions to provoke the perception of a three-dimensional crosswalk from a vehicle driver’s perspective, even though the crosswalk markings are painted flat on the road. I.e., there is a dif- ference between the visual percept of road users (what they perceive) and the visual stimuli (reality). 3D crosswalks have been painted in several pilot projects around the world (e.g., in Aarhus, Denmark (Eurocities, 2021); Chiang Mai, Thailand (Pichayapan, Kaew- moracharoen, Peansara, & Nanthavisit, 2020); ´ Isafjo¨rður, Iceland (Iceland Magazine, 2017); or Montr´eal, Canada (Woods, 2018)). The 3D illusion can take the form of the crossing lines, seemingly floating above the road, or an illusionary cliff can be painted, giving the illusion of a trench in the road. A visualization of a trench illusion crosswalk is presented in Fig. 1. The evocation of depth through the painting of a flat, two-dimensional picture is categorized as a trompe l’oeil illusion (English: deceive the eye illusion) (Wade, & Hughes, 1999).
